text: Digital Egypt for Universities provides educational background on Egyptian history, archaeology, language, religion, objects, and sites. It is useful for orientation and should be cited by page when a specific claim is made.

Isis was a major goddess in ancient Egyptian religion. She was associated with motherhood, protective magic, and the Osiris myth, in which she is the wife of Osiris and mother of Horus. Her worship continued into the Greco-Roman world.
Osiris was an important Egyptian god associated with kingship, death, renewal, and the afterlife. The Osiris cycle connects him with Isis, Horus, and Seth.
Horus was a major Egyptian deity connected with kingship and protection. In the Osiris cycle, Horus is the son of Isis and Osiris and the opponent of Seth.
Seth was an Egyptian god associated in different periods with storms, disorder, deserts, foreign lands, and dangerous power. In the Osiris cycle he is the brother and opponent of Osiris and Horus.
Ramesses II was a king of Egypt in the Nineteenth Dynasty of the New Kingdom. His reign is associated with major building projects, military activity, and the peace treaty with the Hittite kingdom.
Hatshepsut was a woman who ruled as king of Egypt during the Eighteenth Dynasty. Her reign is known for building projects, trade expeditions, and the temple at Deir el-Bahari.
The Old Kingdom is the period of Egyptian history associated with the early pyramid age, centralized kingship, and the construction of major pyramids at sites including Giza and Saqqara.

The New Kingdom was a powerful period of ancient Egyptian history. It included the Eighteenth, Nineteenth, and Twentieth Dynasties and produced rulers such as Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, and Ramesses II.

Egyptian pyramids were royal funerary monuments. Their construction required quarrying, transporting, and placing large stone blocks, along with organized labor, planning, food supply, and administration. The exact methods varied by period and are still studied by Egyptologists.

Ancient Egyptian temples were religious institutions where rituals, offerings, festivals, priestly work, and royal representation took place. They also controlled land, labor, and resources in many periods.
